power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. info.title: Near-Death Experiences and Near-Death-Like Experiences: A Comparative Synthesis and Implications for Their Interpretation

author.affiliation:
Science of Consciousness Research Group -Studium Patavinum
								University of Padua
								
									Italy

text.text: Near-death experiences (NDEs) are most often reported in association with physiologically life-threatening events such as cardiac arrest or coma, but phenomenologically similar reports, near-death-like (NDE-like) experiences, also arise in the absence of a life threat, for example during syncope, deep meditation, hypnosis, and psychedelic states.
This synthesis reviews the evidence on whether the phenomenology, psychological correlates, and aftereffects of NDEs differ from those of NDE-like experiences.
Comparing the largest retrospective survey, a mixed-methods online study, and a within-person psychedelic comparison, consistently indicate broad overlap in core features across contexts.

At the same time, encounters with deceased persons or spiritual entities were reported in 34.7% NDE accounts and none of 25 NDE-like accounts in one exploratory study, and a singlecase comparison found life review, encounters with the deceased, and a threshold or point of no return present only in the NDE.

However, no study was designed to test equivalence, samples were largely self-selected and retrospective, and formal measurement-invariance testing of the instruments in use across etiologies is still lacking.
These constraints caution against concluding phenomenological identity.

The implications of this evidence for neurophysiological, psychological, evolutionary, and metaphysical interpretations are analyzed, and priorities for prospective, preregistered, adequately powered research are outlined.

Near-death experiences (NDEs) are profound episodes of what has been termed disconnected consciousness: vivid, internally generated experience occurring, from an outside observer's perspective, in circumstances of severely reduced responsiveness, most typically during cardiac arrest, pathological coma, or other conditions involving an actual or potential physical threat to life (Martial et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Near-death experiences (NDEs) are profound episodes of what has been termed disconnected consciousness: vivid, internally generated experience occurring, from an outside observer's perspective, in circumstances of severely reduced responsiveness, most typically during cardiac arrest, pathological coma, or other conditions involving an actual or potential physical threat to life <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Martial et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Prototypical features include an impression of leaving the body, movement through a tunnel toward a light, encounter with other beings or deceased relatives, a panoramic review of one's life, intense positive emotion, and a perceived boundary or point of no return.

Reports that are phenomenologically similar in most or all of these respects also occur in contexts that are plainly not life-threatening, during fainting (syncope), sleep-related states, deep meditation, hypnosis, and after administration of psychoactive drugs, principally serotonergic psychedelics but also, in the older pharmacological literature, the N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonist ketamine (Jansen, 1997; Rogo, 1984).
text.formatted: Reports that are phenomenologically similar in most or all of these respects also occur in contexts that are plainly not life-threatening, during fainting (syncope), sleep-related states, deep meditation, hypnosis, and after administration of psychoactive drugs, principally serotonergic psychedelics but also, in the older pharmacological literature, the N-methyl-D-aspartate antagonist ketamine <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Jansen, 1997;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Rogo, 1984)</ref>.

text.text: Following the convention of the literature reviewed here, I refer to the former as NDEs (or, where the context requires, clinically verified NDEs) and the latter as NDE-like experiences.

The coexistence of these two classes of reports poses the central question of this review: does the phenomenology of an NDE depend on the proximity of its trigger to actual physiological death, or can experiences of the same kind arise when life was never in danger?
The question matters for theory.
If NDE features are related to their etiology, explanations may be trigger-specific, for instance in terms of cerebral hypoxia or the neurophysiology of the dying brain.
If NDE features are not related to their etiology, then either very different triggers converge on shared mechanisms, or the source of the experience is not tied to any particular trigger at all.
The comparison is also practically consequential, because NDE-like reports are common in clinical and non-clinical populations, and instruments developed for NDEs are routinely used to classify them.
Three terminological cautions are implicated in what follows.
First, the boundary between NDE and NDE-like experience is definitional rather than natural.
A report is classified as an NDE-like experience by the absence of a documented life threat, and in most studies that absence is established by self-report rather than medical records.

When the primary studies are evaluated below, I accordingly distinguish self-identified life threats, which the experiencer reports but which are not documented in medical records, from medically documented crises; wherever the distinction matters to a study's interpretation, it is stated.
Second, the taxonomy adopted here is defined by objective threat rather than by the experiencer's subjective appraisal.

An individual who was not physiologically close to death but believed at the time that they were dying, as can happen in uncomplicated syncope, a panic attack, or minor trauma, is counted here as an NDE-like experiencer, even though some models deliberately encompass situations that are actual, potential, or merely perceived threats, as NEPTUNE does (Martial et al., 2025), and even though subjective nearness to death may itself shape the phenomenology: some classic reports of NDE features were in fact obtained from patients who were not, medically speaking, near death (Owens et al., 1990).

text.text: Throughout this article, "classical NDE" refers to experiences reported after a self-identified or documented lifethreatening event, and NDE-like to those reported without one, mirroring the usage of the primary studies.
This paper is a narrative synthesis, not a systematic review, and its literature base was assembled as follows.

The primary comparative studies were identified through searches of Europe PMC (which indexes MEDLINE/PubMed content) combining neardeath experience with terms including near-death-like, psychedelic, DMT, ketamine, meditation, hypnosis, syncope, personality, and fear of death, with no date restriction; through forward and backward citation tracing from the comparisons identified; and through the reference lists of recent integrative reviews (Martial et al., 2025) comparisons and controlled elicitations reviewed in Section 3 regardless of publication date.

text.text: The remainder of the article proceeds as follows.

Section 2 sets out the definitional and measurement foundations; Section 3 reviews the phenomenological comparisons across etiologies; Sections 4 through 6 examine candidate discriminating features, psychological correlates, and aftereffects; Section 7 develops a methodological critique; Section 8 considers what the evidence implies, and does not imply, for theoretical interpretation, and closes with discriminating predictions and research designs; and Section 9 offers concluding reflections.
>Definitional and Measurement Foundations
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Definitional and Measurement Foundations</head>

text.text: The concept of an NDE emerged from reports by resuscitated and comatose patients, and only later were instruments created to identify and grade the experiences.
The resulting risk of circularity has been recognized within the field.

On the basis of a case report of a near-death-like experience without any life-threatening condition, Facco and Agrillo (2012)   2018) pointed out that no instrument had been designed for the meditation-induced experiences they studied.
text.formatted: On the basis of a case report of a near-death-like experience without any life-threatening condition, <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Facco and Agrillo (2012)</ref>   <ref type="formula">2018</ref>) pointed out that no instrument had been designed for the meditation-induced experiences they studied.

text.text: The most widely used instrument is the NDE Scale developed by Greyson (1983).
text.formatted: The most widely used instrument is the NDE Scale developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Greyson (1983)</ref>.

text.text: It comprises 16 items grouped into cognitive, affective, paranormal, and transcendental subscales, each scored 0 to 2 for a total range of 0 to 32, with a total score of 7 or above conventionally treated as the threshold for an NDE.
Two features of its development deserve emphasis in the present context.

The scale was constructed from retrospective accounts of self-identified experiencers, a construction sample of 67 participants reporting 73 NDEs (as summarized in Timmermann et al., 2018), whose proximity to death was heterogeneous and, in many cases, not medically documented.
text.formatted: The scale was constructed from retrospective accounts of self-identified experiencers, a construction sample of 67 participants reporting 73 NDEs (as summarized in <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Timmermann et al., 2018)</ref>, whose proximity to death was heterogeneous and, in many cases, not medically documented.

text.text: The Greyson scale was therefore not developed and validated specifically in cardiac-arrest populations, contrary to a common implicit assumption in this literature; it is a scale for grading the content of experiences that people already report as near-death, whatever their context.

Its crosscontext validity, the question of whether a given score means the same thing in a cardiacarrest survivor, a meditator, and a psychedelic user, was not established at the outset and has not been systematically established since.
The psychometric picture is, however, more differentiated than a simple deficit.

In a Rasch scaling validation, Lange, Greyson, and Houran (2004) showed that the NDE Scale satisfactorily fits a unidimensional rating-scale model with interval-level properties, with item semantics invariant across experiencers' gender, current age, age at the time of the NDE, and the intensity and elapsed time of the experience; the same authors extended this validation program in subsequent work (Lange et al., 2015), and the resulting hierarchy of increasingly rare features has proved stable over two decades (Pehlivanova et al., 2026).

text.text: What this work did not do is compare etiologies.

It establishes the scale's internal structure and its invariance across demographic and experiential variables, not its equivalence between, say, cardiac-arrest survivors and meditators, which is the crosspopulation question the present literature requires.

The 20-item Near-Death Experience Content (NDE-C) scale, developed and psychometrically validated by Martial et al. (2020), was designed to improve content coverage and reliability relative to earlier instruments; it is scored 0 to 80 with a conventionally used threshold of 27.

(2020)</ref>, was designed to improve content coverage and reliability relative to earlier instruments; it is scored 0 to 80 with a conventionally used threshold of 27.

text.text: The NDE-C has since been translated and examined in other populations, including a Chinese translation and validation (Li et al., 2024) that was used in the study of Xue et al. (2026) reviewed below.

text.text: Most relevant to the clinical aspect of this field, Stripp and Hvidt (2026) evaluated the psychometric properties of a Danish translation of the NDE-C in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest survivors identified through the Danish Cardiac Arrest Register.

text.text: Of 2,262 invited survivors, 855 responded (37.8%), and 226 participants who reported memories from their cardiac arrest completed the scale.

Internal consistency was excellent (Cronbach's α = .92), and a confirmatory factor analysis supported the intended five-factor structure conceptually, but the global fit indices were mixed, with most falling below conventional thresholds for good fit (CFI = .858, TLI = .831, RMSEA = .093, SRMR = .062).

The authors' own conclusion is that the Danish NDE-C shows strong internal consistency and a preliminary acceptable, although not good, factor structure, and that further psychometric validation is necessary.

The NDE-C is thus a promising but still maturing instrument; neither it nor the Greyson scale has undergone the formal multi-group measurement-invariance testing across etiologies that their cross-context use presupposes (see Section 2.2).
The comparison at the heart of this review inherits these measurement limits.

When a cardiac-arrest survivor and a meditator both score above a threshold on the same scale, what has been demonstrated is a partial overlap in the features the scale samples, not phenomenological identity, and not even equivalence in the features sampled unless the scale functions equivalently in both groups (Putnick & Bornstein, 2016).

text.text: Under the framework of Putnick and Bornstein (2016), comparing observed or latent group means across etiologies presupposes configural invariance (the same factor structure in each group), metric invariance (equal factor loadings), and scalar invariance (equal item intercepts or thresholds), so that a given item endorsement reflects the same level of the latent construct rather than etiology-specific differential item functioning; the Rasch program summarized in Section 2.2 established the first of these requirements in a strong form within single populations, but none of the comparisons reviewed below has tested them across etiological groups.

>Phenomenological Comparisons Across Etiologies
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Phenomenological Comparisons Across Etiologies</head>

text.text: Charland-Verville et al. (2014), in their retrospective survey of 190 self-reported experiencers who scored above the conventional Greyson threshold, found that 140 (73.7%) had undergone a pathological coma of documented anoxic, traumatic, or other etiology, and 50 (26.3%) had lived through a non-life-threatening event.
Neither the intensity of the experience (the Greyson total score) nor the frequency of its content features differed between the "real NDE" and "NDE-like" groups.
Within the "real NDE" group the content did not vary with the cause of coma.
Peacefulness was the most frequently reported feature in all groups (89-93%), and only 2 of 190 participants (about 1%) described a distressing experience.
The authors' conclusion was that "it appears that 'real NDEs' after coma of different etiologies are similar to 'NDE-like' experiences occurring after non-life threatening events" (p. 9).
Two further results of the same study qualify this conclusion and are often overlooked.

First, the recruitment was retrospective and self-selected, largely through organizations and media devoted to near-death experiences, and the authors explicitly caution that such a sample may not represent the experiencer population, noting in addition the ill-defined nature of the non-life-threatening conditions.

Second, when the authors compared their retrospectively recruited anoxic-coma cases with historical data from prospectively studied post-anoxic patients, the retrospectively recruited experiencers reported different content.
Retrospective recruitment, in other words, may itself shape what is reported, a point of first importance for a literature built on retrospective surveys.

Memory characteristics tell a convergent story. Cassol et al. (2019) screened 71 experiencers with the Greyson scale, 48 of whom had lived a real NDE in a life-threatening context and 23 of whom reported an NDE-like experience without a life threat.

(2019)</ref> screened 71 experiencers with the Greyson scale, 48 of whom had lived a real NDE in a life-threatening context and 23 of whom reported an NDE-like experience without a life threat.

text.text: The two subgroups did not differ in the proportion who recalled their experience among their two main self-defining memories (63% and 48%, respectively, a nonsignificant difference), and among the 41 participants who did so, the NDE or NDE-like memory was rated as more central to identity than their other self-defining memories, with the richness of the experience (its Greyson score) associated with that centrality.
The authors concluded that the self-defining status of the memory appears to be tied to its phenomenological content rather than to the circumstances in which it arose.

Related work on the same question found that the memories of NDEs reported by coma survivors carry more phenomenological characteristics than memories of imagined events, and indeed more than memories of real events, indicating that they are recalled as genuine perceptual memories rather than as fantasies (Thonnard et al., 2013).

text.text: The narrative structure of NDE accounts themselves, in turn, has been mapped thematically in cardiac-arrest survivors, yielding a sequence of recurring time-bounded features rather than an undifferentiated report (Cassol et al., 2018).

text.text: The most recent direct comparison comes from a Chinese online sample (Xue et al., 2026), an exploratory mixed-methods study in which 63 participants entered the quantitative analysis, 23 reporting an NDE, 25 an NDE-like experience, and 15 reporting experiences below the threshold of the Chinese NDE-C scale, and 48 provided narratives for thematic analysis.
text.formatted: The most recent direct comparison comes from a Chinese online sample <ref type="bibr">(Xue et al., 2026)</ref>, an exploratory mixed-methods study in which 63 participants entered the quantitative analysis, 23 reporting an NDE, 25 an NDE-like experience, and 15 reporting experiences below the threshold of the Chinese NDE-C scale, and 48 provided narratives for thematic analysis.

text.text: Narratives from the two groups shared recurrent features: out-ofbody experiences, bright light, bodily sensations, emotional changes, and altered perceptual content.

At the same time, NDE narratives showed descriptively higher frequencies of peaceful emotions, personal insights, and panoramic life review, and the single most pronounced group difference concerned encounters: deceased loved ones or spiritual entities appeared in 8 of 23 NDE narratives and in none of the 25 NDE-like narratives, the one difference that remained significant after false-discovery-rate correction in the authors' exploratory tests.

Culturally specific Chinese imagery (references to Guimen Pass, Black and White Impermanence, karmic judgment, and related motifs) was uncommon in both groups (4 of 23 and 1 of 25), a difference that likewise did not survive correction.

The authors stress that their classification rested entirely on self-report without clinical verification, that the groups were partly defined by their NDE-C responses, and that their between-group tests should be read descriptively rather than as confirmatory.

The study therefore supports broad overlap while providing the strongest available, though still exploratory, group-level signal of a content difference, precisely in one of the features discussed in Section 4. et al. (2018) administered intravenous N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) to 13 healthy volunteers in a fixed-order, placebo-controlled, single-blind design, with the Greyson scale as the primary outcome.

(2018)</ref> administered intravenous N,N-dimethyltryptamine (DMT) to 13 healthy volunteers in a fixed-order, placebo-controlled, single-blind design, with the Greyson scale as the primary outcome.

text.text: All 13 participants scored above the NDE threshold after DMT, and the total score was strongly elevated relative to placebo (d = 3.09); 15 of the 16 items were rated higher under DMT, 10 of them significantly so after correction for multiple testing.

In a separate comparison with a gender-and age-matched sample of 13 individuals who had reported an actual NDE after a life-threatening episode, the total scores of the two groups were, in the authors' words, comparable (t(12) = 1.85, p = .089, d = 0.49).
One participant reached the threshold score of 7 in the placebo condition itself.

The comparison is frequently cited as showing that the DMT state and the NDE are statistically indistinguishable; however, a nonsignificant difference between groups of 13 is not evidence of equivalence, no equivalence test was performed, and the design had little power to detect a moderate difference (see Section 7.5).

At the item level, the only feature that differed nominally between the two groups is directly relevant here: the threshold item, "Did you come to a border or point of no return?", was scored higher by the actual NDE group than in the DMT condition (t(12) = 2.74, p = .018 uncorrected, d = 1.07), a large effect that did not survive correction for the 16 items tested.
What the study does establish is that a psychedelic can reliably elicit experiences that clear the conventional NDE threshold.

A unique within-person case analysis was reported by Michael et al. (2023), who interviewed an individual documented as having had a profound NDE during a coma caused by bacterial meningoencephalitis and, years later, an experience with 5-methoxy-DMT.
text.formatted: A unique within-person case analysis was reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Michael et al. (2023)</ref>, who interviewed an individual documented as having had a profound NDE during a coma caused by bacterial meningoencephalitis and, years later, an experience with 5-methoxy-DMT.

text.text: Thematic comparison showed substantial overlap, especially in the major mystical domains such as ego dissolution and the transcendence of time and space (the NDE also shared many characteristics with psychedelic experiences generally, including entering other worlds, encountering entities, synesthesia, and perinatal regression).

Three themes, however, emerged only in the NDE: life review, encountering the deceased, and the threshold or point of no return; the authors note that the NDE included other beings or religious and deceased spirits whereas the 5-methoxy-DMT experience did not, and describe these divergences as potentially the most robust differences between the two states.
It is worth adding that the participant himself judged the two experiences not similar enough to attribute the NDE to endogenous psychedelic activity.

The authors propose, speculatively and with explicit caveats, that different upstream causes (5-HT2A receptor agonism in the psychedelic case, neocortical damage from meningoencephalitis in the other) could produce similar downstream top-down cortical disinhibition.
A single case cannot establish how generally these observations hold, but as a within-person comparison it controls for the reporting style of the experiencer in a way no between-group design can.

The within-person logic was extended to a sample by Martial et al. (2024a), who surveyed 31 adults reporting both an NDE (NDE-C score at or above 27) and a psychedelic experience with lysergic acid diethylamide, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, or mescaline, analyzing the two experiences of each participant with frequentist and Bayesian methods.
text.formatted: The within-person logic was extended to a sample by <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Martial et al. (2024a)</ref>, who surveyed 31 adults reporting both an NDE (NDE-C score at or above 27) and a psychedelic experience with lysergic acid diethylamide, psilocybin, ayahuasca, DMT, or mescaline, analyzing the two experiences of each participant with frequentist and Bayesian methods.

text.text: They found areas of overlap between the experiences in phenomenology, attribution of reality, psychological insight, and enduring effects, together with differentiating features: most notably, the feeling of dying or being dead and disembodiment were reported more often for NDEs, whereas unusual visual and sensory imagery was more pronounced in psychedelic experiences.
Within-person designs of this kind are among the most informative available, because each participant serves as their own control for narrative style and belief.

Van Gordon et al. (2018) followed 12 advanced Buddhist meditators (two-thirds of them monastics, with an average of roughly 28 years of meditation practice) over three years, comparing a death-related meditation reported to induce NDEs (MI-NDE) against two control practices in the same practitioners.
Admission to the MI-NDE condition required a score of 7 or above on the Greyson scale for the most recent such experience, so above-threshold scores were partly guaranteed by the sampling.
MI-NDE sessions nonetheless scored significantly higher than both control conditions.

Strikingly, the mean Greyson scores of both control conditions themselves exceeded the NDE threshold (standard meditation: M = 7.17, SD = 1.34; standard meditation with death contemplation: M = 8.0, SD = 1.28); ordinary meditative states, in other words, averaged above the conventional cutoff.

The embedded qualitative analysis found that participants were consciously aware of experiencing an NDE, retained volitional control over its content and duration, and reported a rich array of non-worldly encounters, alongside features the authors describe as novel relative to ordinary NDE reports.
The authors themselves caution that no instrument was designed for meditation-induced experiences and that the NDE scale may lack specificity in this population.
Hypnosis provides a further analogue.

In an exploratory study, Machado Ferreira, Farinha, and Simões (2022) examined experiences elicited under hypnotic induction and reported that among the 17 participants whose totals met the criterion of 7 or above on the Greyson scale, the resulting profiles were similar to those of classical near-death experiencers in both content and intensity.

Like the meditation evidence, this finding indicates that a conventional NDEinstrument threshold can be crossed in a state that is neither dangerous nor, in the ordinary sense, near to death; the study's exploratory character and its exclusively scale-based comparison should, however, be kept in view.

text.text: Taken together, the comparisons above suggest a short list of features that may The honest summary is that these three features are hypotheses.

They are plausible candidates for markers that co-vary with proximity to death, they are consistently present in the small evidentiary base that bears on them, but no adequately powered, preregistered study has tested whether they discriminate clinically verified NDEs from matched NDElike experiences.

Their present evidentiary weight ranges from one exploratory group comparison to one case study plus one uncorrected item-level difference, and they should be treated as targets for prospective research (Section 8.6) rather than as established differentiators.
The sharpest quantified difference between the populations concerns not the content of the experiences but the psychology of those who report them.
Martial et al.

(2018) compared five groups recruited and screened with the Greyson scale: experiencers whose NDE occurred in a life-threatening context (n = 51), experiencers whose NDE-like experience occurred without one (n = 57), non-experiencers without life threat (n = 20), people who had come close to death without recalling an NDE (n = 50), and healthy controls (n = 50).

On the Creative Experiences Questionnaire, a measure of fantasy proneness, the NDE-like group scored significantly higher than the classical NDE group (d = 0.56), than the non-experiencers without life threat (d = 0.83), and than the healthy controls (d = 1.20).
Fantasy proneness also correlated with Greyson total scores across the sample as a whole (Spearman ρ = .32).
Two details of these results matter for their interpretation.

First, the comparison between the classical NDE group and the people who had faced death without an NDE, a comparison of substantial theoretical interest, was not significant only after Bonferroni correction; uncorrected, the difference had a nominal p of .019 with a medium effect size (d = 0.47), so the finding of no difference should be held loosely.
Second, the classical NDE group did not differ from healthy controls in fantasy proneness.

The overall pattern, a trait elevation specific to the NDE-like reporters, absent in classical NDE reporters, suggests that fantasy proneness may be involved in who reports NDE-like experiences, or in how such experiences are elaborated and narrated, rather than in near-death phenomenology as such.

The authors are explicit that the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference in either direction, that medical documentation of the life-threatening events was lacking, and that fantasy proneness and NDE intensity may partly share item content.
A subsequent multivariate study from the same group complicates this picture.

The largest comparison of enduring effects is the retrospective survey of Sweeney et al. (2022), with 3,192 respondents: 933 who reported a non-drug near-death or other non-ordinary experience, and 2,259 who reported an experience occasioned by a psychedelic (lysergic acid diethylamide, psilocybin, ayahuasca, or DMT).

(2022)</ref>, with 3,192 respondents: 933 who reported a non-drug near-death or other non-ordinary experience, and 2,259 who reported an experience occasioned by a psychedelic (lysergic acid diethylamide, psilocybin, ayahuasca, or DMT).

text.text: Large majorities of both groups attributed a decrease in fear of death to the experience (88% of the non-drug group and 89% of the psychedelic group), and members of both groups rated the experience as highly personally meaningful and spiritually significant; indeed, participants in the non-drug group were more likely to name it the single most meaningful experience of their lives.

Differences between the groups were modest and specific: psychedelic experiencers scored higher on the Greyson scale total (and on the cognitive, affective, and paranormal subscales, whereas on the transcendental subscale the non-drug group scored higher than the psilocybin and LSD groups but lower than the DMT and ayahuasca groups) and were more likely to meet criteria for a complete mystical experience on the Mystical Experiences Questionnaire (55% versus 47%), whereas the non-drug group showed the larger decrease in death avoidance (mean change -2.01 versus -1.43 on the relevant Death Attitude Profile subscale).

The shared outcome, a marked and enduring reduction in death fear, accords with a longer survey tradition documenting lasting changes in beliefs, attitudes, and behavior after NDEs (Groth-Marnat & Summers, 1998) and with the finding that NDE memories are highly central to identity (Cassol et al., 2019).

text.text: These are retrospective self-reports of change, gathered from self-selected online samples and rated before-and-after in a single sitting, so they describe experienced transformation rather than measured trajectories; but the convergence across drug and non-drug groups, and with the smaller prospective literature, is nonetheless striking.
>Methodological Critique
text.formatted: <head n="7." >Methodological Critique</head>

text.text: The NDE/NDE-like distinction is contested at its definitional root.
The label NDE predates its measurement, and the instruments that now operationalize it were built to grade experiences that people already called near-death.
As Facco and Agrillo (2012) observed, other transcendent experiences may rate highly on those same instruments.
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Facco and Agrillo (2012)</ref> observed, other transcendent experiences may rate highly on those same instruments.

text.text: The circularity is not merely abstract.
In several of the studies reviewed above, the groups compared were partly defined by the very scores that were then compared.
Xue et al.

(2026) classified their groups partly by NDE-C responses and accordingly interpreted between-group scale differences descriptively rather than as independent evidence, and Van Gordon et al. (2018) admitted meditators to their NDE condition only if they had already scored above the Greyson threshold.
text.formatted: (2026) classified their groups partly by NDE-C responses and accordingly interpreted between-group scale differences descriptively rather than as independent evidence, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Van Gordon et al. (2018)</ref> admitted meditators to their NDE condition only if they had already scored above the Greyson threshold.

text.text: In such designs, threshold comparisons are partly built into the sampling, and content comparisons inherit the scale's own definition of the phenomenon.

A premise frequently taken for granted in this literature, that the standard instruments were developed and validated in cardiac-arrest populations and are therefore being extrapolated when applied elsewhere, does not survive scrutiny.

The Greyson scale was constructed from retrospective, self-identified accounts of heterogeneous proximity to death (Greyson, 1983), and the NDE-C, although psychometrically stronger, was likewise developed outside any cardiac-arrest-specific sampling frame (Martial et al., 2020).

text.text: The first psychometric evaluation of an NDE instrument in a medically well-defined cardiacarrest cohort, the Danish NDE-C study of Stripp and Hvidt (2026), is recent, was achieved in translation, and returned a mixed factor structure whose authors call for further validation.

With these standards applied, three conclusions about the substantive questions can be graded.

On psychological predispositions, the evidence is tentative and internally complex: two cross-sectional studies from the same group link different combinations of traits and beliefs to the two kinds of reporting, with fantasy proneness tied to NDE-like reporting in univariate analysis (Martial et al., 2018) but to classical NDE recall, alongside Openness, in multivariate analysis, and with spiritual beliefs carrying the NDE-like association (Bicego et al., 2023); all of it is retrospective, without medical verification or causal direction, and includes one nominally significant comparison concealed by correction.

What has been shown is a partial overlap under heterogeneous instruments without invariance testing, with at least one exploratory group difference (encounters with the deceased), one uncorrected item-level difference (the threshold), and one within-person case (life review, deceased, threshold) pointing the other way.
The honest position is that etiological independence is an open empirical question, not an established finding.

text.text: Any theory of NDEs must now explain a package of findings rather than a favorite one.

First, core phenomenology, out-of-body experience, light, encounters, positive affect, otherworldly travel, reliably recurs across radically different triggers: coma and cardiac arrest, non-life-threatening events, syncope, meditation, hypnosis, and psychedelics (Sections 3.1-3.3).
Second, a small set of features may co-vary with proximity to death, the best candidates being encounters with the deceased, life review, and the threshold, each with limited evidence (Section 4).

Third, the reporter groups differ psychologically: cognitive-personality variables, such as fantasy proneness and Openness, and belief systems, such as spiritual beliefs, relate differently to the recall of classical NDEs and of NDE-like experiences (Section 5).
Fourth, the memories of both kinds of experience are recalled as perceptually real and are central to identity (Cassol et al., 2019; Thonnard et al., 2013).

text.text: Fifth, both kinds are followed by similar, subjectively profound aftereffects (Section 6).
A theory earns consideration in proportion to the range of these constraints it addresses.

The most developed integrative proposal is the model of Martial et al. (2025), the Neurophysiological Evolutionary Psychological Theory Understanding Near-Death Experience (NEPTUNE), which frames the NDE as a cascade of concomitant psychological and neurophysiological processes within an evolutionary framework.

text.text: At the neurophysiological level, the model holds that core features can result from impaired cerebral blood flow causing systemic hypotension, hypoxia, and hypercapnia resulting in acidosis, and from increased neuronal excitability causing dysregulation of key neurotransmitter systems (Martial et al., 2025, p. 298).

text.text: It is essential to read this model correctly in the present context.
NEPTUNE is explicitly pitched at near-death experiences in the broad sense of experiences arising in situations that involve an actual or potential physical threat, or that are perceived as such.

It is therefore not an arrest-specific account that cross-trigger similarity would refute; it is precisely a convergent account, one in which multiple physiological routes funnel into shared downstream processes.

For the taxonomy of Section 1, this also means that NEPTUNE, as a model of actual, potential, and perceived threats, spans the very boundary this review draws between NDE and NDE-like experiences, and it predicts that perceived-threat experiences should share the phenomenology of actual-threat ones, a testable position. What does the cross-trigger phenomenological overlap imply for these models?
It constrains, rather than refutes, neurophysiological explanation.

It rules out explanations that require a single life-threatening trigger, cerebral hypoxia alone, or cardiac arrest alone, as sufficient causes of the phenomenology, because the phenomenology demonstrably also occurs without them.

But it is exactly what convergent models anticipate: if disparate triggers share downstream targets, a disinhibited cortex, an unstable arousal boundary, perturbed self-processing at the temporoparietal junction, then phenomenological similarity across triggers is a prediction, not an anomaly, of the neurophysiological family of accounts.
Psychological accounts explain the same constraints differently.

Expectancy and cultural-schema approaches predict that content should be assembled from available cultural materials and should vary with them; the finding that culturally specific imagery is uncommon yet interpretively salient in Chinese narratives (Xue et al., 2026) is consistent with a construction in which culture shapes the reading of the experience more than its raw ingredients.

Some authors read the evidence of cardiac-arrest NDEs as indicating that consciousness can persist and function when the brain, by available measures, cannot, and hence that NDEs mark the separability of mind from brain (e.g., Angeli-Faez et al., 2025); others argue that nothing about NDEs is beyond the reach of established neuroscience (e.g., Mobbs & Watt, 2011).

text.text: The evidence reviewed here does not adjudicate between these positions, and it is important to be clear about why.

Cross-trigger phenomenological similarity is equally consistent with shared brain mechanisms reached by different routes and with a non-physicalist account on which the brain is one route among several by which the same kind of experience becomes accessible; the data underdetermine the ontology.

What can be said is methodological: a metaphysical interpretation acquires scientific standing exactly when it generates independently testable predictions, most obviously, prospective tests of veridical perception under physiologically documented conditions, with preregistered targets and blinded coding.
No completed test with verified target hits is part of the present evidence base.

The two prospective studies that embedded such tests during resuscitation, AWARE I and AWARE II, yielded no verified identification of the hidden visual targets; in AWARE II, no participant identified the visual image and only one of 28 interviewed survivors identified the auditory stimulus, with low survival and the rarity of reportable experiences limiting the tests (Parnia et al., 2014 (Parnia et al., , 2023)).

text.text: Survival or transmission interpretations should therefore be treated in a scientific context as philosophical possibilities held to that standard, not as findings.
The competing accounts can be set to work.

(1) Trigger-specific versus convergent neurophysiology: if content tracks etiology, feature rates (life review, deceased encounters, threshold) should differ systematically between clinically verified NDE and matched NDE-like groups; if convergence is correct, such differences should be small or absent while shared features should co-occur with shared neural signatures.

The decisive design is a prospective, preregistered comparison of cardiac-arrest survivors recruited through resuscitation registers (in the manner of Stripp & Hvidt, 2026, and Rousseau et al., 2023) with NDE-like experiencers sampled prospectively from well-defined non-life-threatening triggers without circular scale-threshold preselection (or matched on latent trait intensity outside the candidate discriminating items), feature-level coding performed blind to group, and equivalence bounds set in advance (Lakens, 2017).

text.text: What is well supported?

Experiences that clear the conventional NDE thresholds arise readily outside life-threatening contexts, after psychedelics, in meditation and hypnosis, in syncope, and in everyday non-dangerous events; their phenomenology broadly overlaps with that of NDEs reported after medically documented crises; the memories of both are recalled as real and are central to identity; and both are followed by subjectively profound aftereffects, most prominently a reduced fear of death.

This much rests on multiple methods, retrospective surveys, mixed-methods narrative analysis, placebocontrolled pharmacology, within-person comparison, and single-case analysis, and on several research groups, even if those groups partially overlap and none of the comparisons was designed for equivalence.
What is tentatively supported?

A short list of candidate discriminators, encounters with the deceased (one exploratory group difference), life review (one within-person case), and the threshold (one within-person case and one uncorrected item-level difference), and an incompletely mapped pattern of psychological correlates, in which fantasy proneness, Openness, and spiritual beliefs relate differently to the two kinds of reporting across two cross-sectional studies from the same group (Martial et al., 2018; Bicego et al., 2023).

text.text: What is currently unknown is the central question itself: whether phenomenological content is independent of etiology.

No equivalence test, no measurement-invariance test across etiologies, and no adequately powered prospective comparison exists; at present, both a strong claim of difference and a strong claim of identity outrun the evidence.
Nonsignificant group differences, in particular, should not be mistaken for demonstrated equivalence.
Scientific conclusions and philosophical implications should be kept distinct.

The reviewed evidence constrains theories: any account must explain overlap, candidate discriminators, trait-and-belief differences, memory quality, and aftereffects at once, and purely trigger-specific neurophysiological stories are, on current evidence, insufficient.

But the same evidence does not select between a completed neurophysiological account, a psychological-construction account, and a metaphysical account of consciousness; that selection awaits discriminating, preregistered tests of the kind sketched above, and it may not be fully resolvable by phenomenological comparison at all.

The priorities follow directly: prospective recruitment through medical registers with documented crises and matched comparison groups; preregistration of hypotheses, feature definitions, and analysis plans (Nosek et al., 2018); cross-cultural sampling with culturally validated instruments; psychometric revalidation of the existing scales and formal measurement-invariance testing across etiologies; blinded coding of narratives; adequately powered comparisons with explicit equivalence tests; and prospective longitudinal measurement of aftereffects.

text.text: If the three candidate features survive that program, the NDE/NDE-like distinction acquires empirical content; if they do not, the distinction will have been shown to be, in phenomenological terms, an artifact of our categories rather than a fact about the experiences.
Either result would be a genuine advance over the present state, in which the field's central comparison remains, for the most part, untested at the standard it now knows how to meet.

In multivariate logistic regressions, the recall of a classical NDE was associated with Openness to Experience and with fantasy proneness, whereas the recall of an NDE-like experience was specifically associated with the endorsement of spiritual beliefs; a discriminant analysis classified only about a third of participants correctly.

(2018) found uniquely elevated in NDE-like reporters in univariate analysis, fantasy proneness, reappears in Bicego et al. (2023) as a correlate of classical NDE recall once traits and beliefs are modeled jointly, with spiritualbeliefs carrying the NDE-like association.

Retrospective recruitment, self-report, and the absence of causal inference apply to both studies, and both come from the same research group, so the pattern should be treated as the best-available, not an established, disposition profile.Other candidate traits have been linked to NDE intensity elsewhere: for example, trait absorption was associated with NDE-scale scores in the DMT studyof Timmermann et al. InTimmermann et al. (2018), one participant reached the threshold under placebo.
A cutoff that classifies deep relaxation and saline solution as near-death experiences at non-trivial rates cannot, by itself, carry much evidential weight in comparisons between states.

Apparent content equivalence between NDEs and NDE-like states may therefore be partly an artifact of threshold permissiveness: passing a liberal cutoff demonstrates partial feature overlap, not identity.

7.4 Sampling, Reporting, and Cultural Constraints The evidence base is dominated by convenience and self-selected samples, recruited through near-death-interest organizations (Charland-Verville et al., 2014), online panels (Xue et al., 2026; Martial et al., 2024a), or crowd-sourcing platforms, and by retrospective report, in some cases decades after the event.
Retrospection is not a neutral window.

Charland-Verville et al. (2014) themselves found that retrospectively recruited experiencers reported different content than prospectively studied ones, and Sweeney et al. (2022) measured before-and-after change retrospectively, in a single sitting, which measures experienced change rather than actual trajectories.

Subgroup sizes are generally small (ranging from 12 to 57 in the direct multi-participant comparisons, aside from the n = 140 coma cohort of Charland-Verville et al., 2014), and corrections for multiple testing are applied inconsistently across studies.
Cultural framing is a further, under-explored moderator.

In the only direct comparison conducted outside Western samples, culturally specific imagery was uncommon but its interpretation, what encounters and transitions mean, was evidently shaped by the surrounding culture (Xue et al., 2026).
